subtype: Approach: asking for guidance on a project or recommendation [Action]
passage: At a university in a small Dutch town, Mei wanted a professor who had taught a good seminar to guide a research project on river pollution. Mei wrote a one-page outline first, with the question, a rough method and two sources. Kofi read it over coffee and said to cut the second aim, so it was tighter. Then Mei knocked on the office door. "Could you look at this outline and tell me what you think? I am not asking you to supervise yet, only for feedback." The professor read for a while, said the method was solid but the scope was wide, and suggested one paper to read before next month. Mei wrote it down and said thank you.

qa.q: What did Mei put in the one-page outline?
qa.a: The outline had the question, a rough method and two sources.

qa.q: What did Mei want from the professor, and why did Mei avoid asking for supervision yet?
qa.a: Mei wanted honest advice without pressing for a promise, and hoped to make the request easy for the professor to answer.

qa.q: What could Mei try next, and why?
qa.a: Mei could revise the outline using the advice and send it back with a short thanks, because it shows the feedback was used and may lead to further help.

qa.q: How might the professor see a student who arrives with a short outline?
qa.a: The professor can respond to something concrete in a short time, and is not pushed into a commitment.

grounding: A student asks a professor who taught well for project advice, brings a short outline and asks for feedback rather than a promise.

subtype: Approach: asking for guidance on a project or recommendation [Action]
passage:
The physics department's research corridor smelled of solder. Ojas knocked on Dr Zeenat Hussain's open door at 4 p.m., the time she had agreed to.
He had taken her optics course last year and liked how she answered 'why' questions. Now he had an idea for a summer project: measuring air pollution with cheap light sensors on hostel rooftops.
'I've put it on one page,' he said, handing it over. 'The question, the method, what I'd need. I'm not asking you to supervise it. I just wanted your opinion on whether the method makes sense.'
She read it slowly, pen in hand. 'Your sensors will drift with temperature. You'll need a way to calibrate them.' She circled a line. 'And three rooftops won't be enough to say anything.'
Ojas wrote it all down. 'Thank you. I'll fix those and send you a new page next week, if that's okay.'
'Send it,' she said. 'I'm curious now.'

qa.q: What was Ojas's summer project idea?
qa.a: Measuring air pollution with cheap light sensors on hostel rooftops.

qa.q: Why did Ojas say 'I'm not asking you to supervise it', and how might he have felt?
qa.a: He felt a bit nervous and wanted Dr Hussain to feel free to give honest feedback without any pressure to commit.

qa.q: What should Ojas do with the feedback?
qa.a: Fix the calibration and add more rooftops, then send the new page as promised, showing the advice was used.

qa.q: How might Dr Hussain see the one-page outline?
qa.a: She finds it easy to give quick, useful feedback and becomes curious, since no promise was demanded.

grounding: Shows a student asking a former teacher for feedback on a research outline, not a promise, and getting specific advice and interest.

subtype: Approach: asking for guidance on a project or recommendation [Action]
passage:
Subject: Asking for your advice on a project outline
Dear Professor Devika Rao,
I'm Vaibhav from your Indian Economy course last semester. Your lectures on rural credit were the reason I chose economics as my major.
I'm planning a small summer project: interviewing twenty women's self-help groups near my home town about how they decide on loans. I've attached a one-page outline with my question, method and timeline.
I'm not asking you to supervise it or to write anything for me. I would be grateful for any comments on whether the method is realistic, especially the number of groups. Fifteen minutes in your office hours, or a short reply by email, would both be wonderful.
If you're too busy this month, I completely understand.
Thank you,
Vaibhav Joshi

qa.q: How many self-help groups did Vaibhav plan to interview?
How does Vaibhav seem to feel about Professor Rao?
qa.a: Vaibhav admires the professor, crediting the lectures on rural credit for the choice of major, and feels hopeful but careful not to impose.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do while waiting for a reply?
qa.a: Try the interview questions with one group near home, so there is something concrete to ask about.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao feel reading this email?
qa.a: The professor would likely feel pleased and respected, since it asks for specific feedback and leaves an easy way to say no.

grounding: Shows a student writing to a professor who taught well, sharing a one-page outline and asking for feedback rather than a promise.
